doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The rhythm changes train wreck at a festival
summary: At an indoor festival the rhythm section and horn played different forms; Buster Williams laughed, and Gates learned to stop and start over.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: You ever have any train wrecks?

Oh, big ones man. The one that I can think of offhand that comes to me, it’s funny and it was a real learning experience for me. I got put with a quartet. Piano, bass, drums and an alto player, to do a festival. An indoor festival. And everything was going fine. We were about 3/4 of the way through the set. And it’s like this it’s bass, drums, alto, piano. And I turned to the band and I say, “rhythm changes in E flat.” Then I turned to the audience © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

and say, “George and Ira Gershwin wrote a song called ‘I Got Rhythm.’ Lester Young composed a melody over ‘I Got Rhythm’ and he called it ‘Lester Leaps In.’ The lyrical version is called ‘I Got the Blues.’” I turned to the band and say, “one/two/one-two-three- four.” Now maybe they weren’t listening. But the bass player — you know where this is going already, right? The bass player and the drummer start to play rhythm changes. And the piano player and the alto player are playing the blues. Now that works for about two measures. Then it kind of goes in different directions. Now I’m trying to sing [sings] I got the blues and I don’t know how to lose them/I got the blues and I don’t know what to do. Boom. That’s where it changes. And I feel this shift happen. So I’m leaning into the bass player so I can hear “I Got Rhythm” and these guys are playing something else. And I’m trying to give them the signal or something, and it’s not happening. So by the time I get into the solo, they get it. And we hook up. So we finished the set and Buster Williams and his group are coming up next. But Buster is sitting in the like the fourth row. And when we come off and they’re going up, he’s laughing so hard, and I had met him a little bit before that. He’s cracking up. He said, “man, that was the funniest thing I ever saw.” He says, “you were bound and determined to sing ‘I Got Rhythm.’” So he said, “but you know it worked.” He said, “because some people didn’t hear it, they didn’t get it; some people thought hmm, this is interesting; or some people knew what was happening, maybe only a few, the musicians might have known. So yeah, that was very uncomfortable. There was probably like 1,500 people in the audience. But what I learned was, if that happens, stop. Start over. So what, we made a mistake. You know? We breathe. We walk around, sometimes we trip. Lord Buckley said, “to err is human and to forgive is a gasser.” So stop, start over.
Yeah. I mean I always tell my students if you make a mistake keep going. But you’re describing something a little different.
